title: Season 1, Ep 6: Distributed inference scaling
oneliner: Production LLMs must scale automatically for application teams - and the two technologies to know are vLLM (paged attention, KV caching) and TensorRT-LLM (NVIDIA-optimized, multi-region distribution).
says: As an AI infrastructure architect you provision LLMs on AWS, Azure, or IBM Cloud, and they must scale automatically so application teams can use them effectively. Two major technologies make this work: vLLM (virtual large language model), which uses the Hugging Face ecosystem and scales the model with paged attention and KV caching to cut latency and increase speed; and TensorRT-LLM, which comes from NVIDIA and increases speed while reducing latency by distributing the model across regions. He promises a blueprint for the classic-to-AI infrastructure transition at the end of the season.
explained: Scaling inference is the daily reality after the GPU shopping is done. A single model server melts (overloads and fails) under real application traffic, so the serving layer becomes the critical piece. vLLM's contribution is memory efficiency: paged attention manages the KV cache - the model's working memory of the conversation so far - in pages, like an operating system manages RAM, so one GPU serves far more concurrent users.

TensorRT-LLM attacks from the compilation side: NVIDIA compiles the model into a form its GPUs execute fastest, and supports distributing very large models across nodes and regions. The architect's takeaway is that 'deploy the model' is really 'choose and operate a serving stack' - and this choice, more than the model itself, decides your latency and your token bill.
takeaway: Model serving is its own discipline: vLLM for efficient GPU memory and concurrency, TensorRT-LLM for NVIDIA-optimized, distributed speed.
